text: The `delivery` seed's `Review` gate is fix-and-pass, not adjudicate-and-reject. Its prompt says "Fix every Critical and High finding, keep the build green, and commit. Report passed=true only when nothing Critical or High is left UNRESOLVED", so the gate REPAIRS the work itself and then reports success. Its own failing back-edge (`Review -> Implement`, `passed=false`, `carry:["findings"]`) is therefore almost unreachable: the only way to take it is for the reviewer to fail at fixing, not to decide the work is wrong. This is the opposite of `DoDGate`, whose prompt correctly says "MEASURE ONLY -- do not fix". CONTROLLED EVIDENCE, four real runs: with the shipped fix-and-pass prompt the back-edge fired 0/3 times (parselimit, safepath2, and an early ratelimit attempt) and every node was visited exactly once. Replacing ONLY that node's prompt with an adjudicate-only one -- same graph, same edges, same goal, same model -- fired the edge on the first try: `Review#1 FAIL -> Implement`, `Implement` revisited 2/4, converged, `complete`. The prompt is the variable; the topology was never the problem. Two further defects in the same node: `findings` is NOT in the schema's `required` list, so a failing Review can legally carry an empty or absent `findings` array and re-enter `Implement` with nothing actionable; and the fix-and-pass wording also makes `Review` a silent second implementer, so work lands that the trace attributes to review rather than to `Implement`. Discriminating check (RED on the current seed, GREEN after): assert that for every seed under `scripts/seeds/`, any node of kind `gate` (a) has a prompt containing a measure-only directive and NOT an instruction to fix/commit, and (b) declares every field named in any outgoing edge's `carry` inside its schema's `required` array. Both halves are RED on `delivery.json` today.

`DoDGate`'s failing edge is `carry:["unmetCriteria"]`, and `unmetCriteria` is typed `array of string` — bare criterion IDs. The node's schema ALSO produces `criteria[]`, which is `required` and whose items carry `{id, verdict, evidence}` where `evidence` is the adjudicator's cited artifact proof (file:line, command output, test result). So the back-edge drops the required, evidence-bearing field and carries the optional, contentless one. A re-entered `Implement` therefore learns WHICH criterion failed but never WHY, and has to re-derive the diagnosis the gate already did. That is the difference between a loop that converges and a loop that burns its visit cap: the carry is the only channel the graph has for turning a gate failure into actionable input, and here it is throttled to a list of IDs. Worse, `unmetCriteria` is not in `required`, so a failing DoDGate can legally carry nothing at all. Note the same shape appears on `Review` (see review-gate-repairs-instead-of-routing). Discriminating check (RED on the current seed, GREEN after): assert that for every seed, every gate's failing back-edge carries at least one field that the node's schema marks `required` AND whose type is not `array of string` (i.e. it carries structured per-item detail, not bare identifiers). RED on `delivery.json` for both `Review -> Implement` and `DoDGate -> Implement`.

`validateGraph(next, prev, cursor)` in `scripts/graph-core.mjs` silently degrades to permissive when called with one argument. Both lock-enforcement branches are guarded on `prev` being truthy: the 'invariants.mustCross is set but invariants.lockedHash was never stamped' error and the 'invariants were modified — they are frozen at approval' error. This is deliberate for pre-approval, where no prior graph exists — but nothing at the call site distinguishes pre-approval from validating an already-approved graph, and the permissive path is the DEFAULT one you get by forgetting an argument. Observed while authoring a run by hand: `validateGraph(g)` returned `[]` for a graph with `mustCross` set and NO `lockedHash`, and `scaffold-loom.cjs` then rejected the very same graph with 'invariants.mustCross is set but invariants.lockedHash was never stamped'. Two components disagreed about whether the graph was valid, and the more permissive one is the easier call to write. A validator whose safety depends on the caller remembering a second positional argument fails open. Discriminating check (RED today, GREEN after): call `validateGraph(g)` with a single argument on a graph carrying `approved:true` (or a non-empty `invariants.mustCross`) and no `lockedHash`, and assert the returned violation list is NON-empty — an approved graph validated without a prior must not pass. Returns `[]` today.

The `delivery` seed's terminal edge `PR -> Done` is `when: "always"`, so the run reports `complete` whether or not a PR was actually opened. Observed in the `ratelimit` run: `PR#1` returned prUrl="BLOCKED: no PR opened. ... has no git remote" -- an honest, correct refusal to invent an external side effect -- and the interpreter routed it straight to `Done` and stamped the run `complete`. Every gate had genuinely passed, so this is not a soundness hole in the gates; it is a reporting hole in the terminal. `complete` is the word an operator reads as "delivered", and here nothing was delivered. Note the seed already has the vocabulary to express this: `DoDGate` and `Review` both branch on a boolean and route failures backwards, while `PR` -- the only node whose job is an irreversible outward-facing action -- is the one node with no verdict at all. Discriminating check (RED today, GREEN after): assert that in every seed, the node immediately preceding `terminal` reports a success field in its schema `required` and its edge to the terminal is conditional on that field, so a blocked delivery cannot terminate as `complete`. RED on `delivery.json`: `PR`'s schema has no boolean and its outgoing edge is unconditional.
